newsitem.title: USA: Dlr bounces back to end higher in cross-driven US.
newsitem.headline: Dlr bounces back to end higher in cross-driven US.

text.p: The dollar bounced back from sharp losses on Tuesday to end significantly higher against the yen in U.S. trade on Wednesday in a cross-driven session.

Ignoring more warnings from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Japan's trade surplus with the U.S., dealers pushed the dollar higher through sales of yen and marks, sparking dollar short-covering in the afternoon.
"I think the market got a little too short. They sold further into it and they set themselves up for a giant short squeeze," said Alfonso Alejo, corporate foreign exchange manager at Sakura Bank Ltd.
The dollar ended the day at 123.25/35 yen, up from 122.30/40 at the open. The dollar also improved to 1.6770/80 marks against 1.6712/15 in early trade.
The dollar's upward momentum began overseas when the Bank of Japan's quarterly Tankan report on business confidence showed surprisingly mixed results.

Expectations of a strong report had pushed the dollar sharply lower against the yen on Tuesday. And while some improvement in the mood of Japan's corporations was evident, the survey also highlighted insecurity about the future.
"The market was looking for more strength in the Tankan report than they got," said Dominick Presa, chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dresdner Bank.

The key index rose to plus two in March from minus three in the previous survey last November, the first positive reading since November 1991. But this strength contrasted sharply with the mood among non-manufacturers, whose index plunged beyond most expectations.
In U.S. trade, the dollar's strength persisted with the help of large hedge fund purchases, active sales of mark/lira and mark/Swiss, as well as Swiss/yen buying.
Also helping the dollar on Wednesday, dealers said, were several news reports which raised the possiblity of more interest rate hikes from the Fed.

An article in the Washington Post quoted Fed Governor Laurence Meyer as saying the U.S. economy was "really strong" and suggested that recent data pointed to another credit tightening from the central bank next month.
A newswire report on Wednesday, quoting unnamed Fed sources, also raised the prospect for further Fed rate rises.

The market largely ignored comments from prominent U.S. economist Fred Bergsten, who said that by highlighting trade issues with Japan, the Treasury Department was implicitly calling for a stronger yen.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said that a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus could cause friction between Japan and the United States.
"Bergsten's and Rubin's comments didn't even budge the dollar," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I think the market got caught leaning the wrong way," Chandler added, referring to an overabundance of short-dollar positions.
Dealers said position squaring ahead of Friday's key nonfarm payrolls report and Rubin's trip to Japan later in the week clouded trade throughout the Wednesday session.

In other trade, the dollar ended flat at 1.4435/45 Swiss francs. The British pound edged lower to $1.6425/35 from $1.6430/40 while the Australian dollar ended a tad lower at $0.7843/48 versus $0.7845/55.
The dollar dropped to Canadian $1.3850/55 from C$1.3858/63 at the open.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
